newsitem.title: USA: Young Americans still drinking less coffee - P&G.
newsitem.headline: Young Americans still drinking less coffee - P&G.

text.p: Tie-dyed shirts, clogs and John Travolta have all managed to make a comeback in the 90's, but so far the coffee industry has been unable to reverse a 20-year slide in consumption by younger drinkers.
"We've seen a decline in consumption steadily among young people," said Ted Woehrle, coffee marketing director for Procter & Gamble Co, parent company of leading U.S. brand Folgers Coffee.
"And if we don't turn it around, we're going to see our industry in a world of hurt in another decade or two."
But he added, "If relics from the 1970s can do it (make a comeback), I think coffee can too."
In 1970, Americans between the ages of 20 and 24 years drank about 1.75 cups of coffee per day, more than triple the approximently half of cup they drink today.

The trend, due to the growing popularity of carbonated soft drinks among the younger set, is causing concern in the U.S. coffee industry, which is meeting at the National Coffee Association convention here this week.
To combat the decline, the industry needs to develop products and marketing with what Woehrle called "the three Cs": A cool image, creamy taste and convenience.
"We need to make it cool to drink coffee again," he said. "Our image is stodgy and boring."
For budding coffee drinkers, Woehrle said manufacturers need to focus on sweetened coffees, with plenty of milk to counter the idea of coffee as a bitter, acquired taste.
"We need to focus on sweeter, creamy coffees for younger consumers," he said. "It is a great way to get them in the door and (start) developing a taste for coffee."

In order to make coffee a more convenient beverage to drink and buy, the industry should look at other retail outlets including fast food restaurants, vending machines and more coffee bars and kiosks.
Ready-to-drink coffees and easy-to- prepare soluble products will also help to change the image of coffee as a daily make-at-home brew.

Woehrle said early evidence shows that efforts to impliment "the three Cs" is beginning to pay off. Consumption by 20 to 24 year-olds rose modestly in 1996 to 0.55 cup per day, from 0.47 cup in 1995 and is expected to make further gains in 1997.
